analyses.name: noise
observations: Noise residual analysis evaluated using Gaussian low-pass filter (sigma=1.00).
Global mean absolute residual is 3.48 on a 0–255 scale (residual standard deviation: 14.12, signed mean: 0.00).
Median absolute residual is 0.00; 95th percentile is 22.00, and 99th percentile is 75.00 (peak observed: 166.00).
Residual intensity varies across spatial regions (regional mean range: 1.90 to 6.27, spread: 4.37). This can reflect varying edge density, texture detail, or localized processing.
Higher residual magnitudes naturally concentrate along edges, textures, and high-frequency structures where the low-pass filter suppresses sharp transitions.
Noise residual analysis examines high-frequency deviations from a low-pass baseline; it does not classify an image as real or fake, and cannot prove manipulation or AI generation.
limitations: Noise residual patterns are heavily influenced by high-frequency image content, sharp edges, and detailed textures.
Image processing operations such as JPEG compression, downsampling, sharpening, and denoising alter noise residual distributions.
Uniform or non-uniform noise residuals do not establish whether an image is authentic, edited, or synthetic.
Residual analysis depends on the chosen filtering model and smoothing parameter (sigma=1).
Sensor noise characteristics vary widely across camera models, ISO settings, and lighting conditions.

analyses.name: frequency
observations: 2D Fast Fourier Transform computed using Hann windowing on 343x361 luminance matrix.
Spectral energy distribution: Low frequency (r < 0.10): 22.41%, Mid frequency (0.10 <= r < 0.40): 47.04%, High frequency (r >= 0.40): 30.56%.
Spectral centroid is 0.367 (normalized radial frequency) with normalized spectral entropy of 0.767.
Spectral energy is distributed across both lower and higher spatial frequencies, reflecting a combination of structural content and fine detail.
Frequency domain analysis evaluates spatial-frequency energy distribution via 2D FFT; it does not classify an image as real or fake, and cannot prove AI generation or manipulation.
limitations: Frequency domain patterns are strongly governed by image semantic content, sharp edges, and detailed textures.
Lossy compression algorithms (such as JPEG DCT quantization), sharpening, downsampling, and denoising alter high-frequency spectral roll-off.
Natural photographs, digital artwork, and generative AI outputs can exhibit overlapping frequency characteristics depending on resolution, content, and post-processing.
2D FFT evaluates global spatial frequencies and does not isolate localized spatial manipulations or splices.
